headline.title: OpenAI's Jalapeño chip beats Nvidia, reshapes AI.
headline.summary: OpenAI unveiled its first in-house AI inference chip, Jalapeño, claiming superior speed and efficiency over Nvidia's flagship GPUs. The chip promises cheaper, faster tokens and a tighter design loop, while the broader industry race for custom silicon intensifies.

stories.title: OpenAI's Jalapeño chip beats Nvidia, reshapes AI.
stories.toc_summary: OpenAI's first custom inference chip claims 3.6x speed and 1.9x efficiency over Nvidia's best, signaling a shift in AI compute strategy.
stories.quick_take: OpenAI has published first benchmarks for its custom inference chip, Jalapeño, built with Broadcom. The chip, rated at 700 watts, outperforms Nvidia's 1200-watt flagships by answering up to 3.6x faster and delivering 1.9x more work per watt [1]. Leveraging its upcoming Astra model and Codex, OpenAI designed the chip in just nine months [1][2]. While not for sale, two more generations are planned, aiming for data centers by end of year and production ramp into 2027 [1]. This move joins Google, Anthropic, Amazon, and Microsoft in a race for custom silicon to cut costs and boost performance [1][2].

bullets.label: Chip specs:
bullets.text: 700W chip beats Nvidia's 1200W options, with 3.6x faster responses and 1.9x more work per watt [1].

bullets.label: Design speed:
bullets.text: Created in nine months using Astra and Codex, from first design to manufacturing-ready [1].

bullets.label: Internal use:
bullets.text: OpenAI will not sell the chip, citing huge internal demand, and still relies on Nvidia for training [1].

bullets.label: Next steps:
bullets.text: Two more generations in development, with deployment later this year and production ramp through 2027 [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: Owning silicon is becoming key to AI leadership, cutting dependency on Nvidia and enabling optimized designs for future models. If Jalapeño holds up, OpenAI gains a significant cost and speed edge in the race for agentic AI [1].

stories.title: China's humanoid robots break world records, alarm Europe.
stories.toc_summary: At the World Robot Conference, humanoids sprinted faster than Bolt and jumped 2.88m, while Chinese giants like JD.com sell them online—signaling a robotics inflection point.
stories.quick_take: At the Robot Games in Peking, a humanoid ran 100m in 9.32 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt, and another jumped 2.88m high—feats no human has matched [1]. The event attracted 2056 robots from 666 teams across 16 countries [1]. Prof. Alois Knoll from TU München confirmed the feats are real, not simulations, and highlighted 50 humanoid manufacturers at the World Robot Conference [1]. Chinese giants like JD.com now sell humanoids online, and automakers BYD, Xiaomi, and Nio are entering the space, leveraging mass production [1]. Germany risks falling behind on tempo, despite strengths in fine mechanics [1].

bullets.label: Record-breaking feats:
bullets.text: Humanoid sprints: 9.32s for 100m; high jump: 2.88m [1].

bullets.label: Mega event:
bullets.text: 2056 robots, 666 teams, 16 countries, 51 disciplines; 300 exhibitors at the conference [1].

bullets.label: Chinese dominance:
bullets.text: JD.com sells humanoids online; automakers like BYD and Xiaomi build them, leveraging mass production [1].

bullets.label: Germany's gap:
bullets.text: Prof. Knoll urges more startups and a five-year horizon; current pace is too slow [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: 2026 is to robotics what 2022 was to AI. China's ecosystem-led approach is setting the pace, and Europe's niche strength in fine mechanics cannot compensate for lack of speed and long-term investment [1].

stories.title: Waymo brings robotaxis to Munich, Europe's first.
stories.toc_summary: Waymo will begin mapping and testing in Munich in coming weeks, targeting a fully autonomous ride service by end of 2027—a direct challenge to Germany's auto industry.
stories.quick_take: Waymo is expanding to Europe for the first time, choosing Munich as its entry point [1]. The company will start with mapping, testing, and calibrating its Waymo Driver on European roads, with a fully autonomous ride service planned for late 2027 [1]. Having driven millions of autonomous miles in US cities like Phoenix and San Francisco, Waymo is now bringing its technology to the heart of Germany's auto industry, competing in BMW's home city [1].

bullets.label: Timeline:
bullets.text: Mapping and testing start in coming weeks; service launch expected end of 2027 [1].

bullets.label: First European city:
bullets.text: Munich, Germany, marks Waymo's initial foray into Europe [1].

bullets.label: Experience:
bullets.text: Millions of autonomous miles already logged in Phoenix, SF, and LA [1].

bullets.label: Strategic move:
bullets.text: Directly challenges German automakers in their home market [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Waymo's entry could pressure European regulators and automakers to accelerate autonomous vehicle adoption, potentially reshaping mobility markets.

stories.title: Figure releases largest robot dataset, Index.
stories.toc_summary: Figure's Index dataset includes 16M videos from real-world collection, aiming to train household robots, with a $1B commitment to data and compute.
stories.quick_take: Figure has come out of stealth with Index, claiming the largest robot training dataset in the world, collected from real-world interactions rather than scraped from the internet [1]. The dataset includes 16 million videos, with 264,000 app downloads in over 100 countries, and $15 million already paid to contributors [1]. Figure plans to commit over $1 billion to data and compute over the next 12 months, aiming for household robots that can perform a wide range of tasks [1]. This move underscores the growing importance of physical data in AI, alongside other startups like Skild AI and Generalist [1].

bullets.label: Dataset scale:
bullets.text: 16M videos, 264k app downloads, $15M paid out [1].

bullets.label: Real-world collection:
bullets.text: Data comes from physical interactions, not internet scraping [1].

bullets.label: Investment:
bullets.text: $1B+ committed to data and compute over the next year [1].

bullets.label: Goal:
bullets.text: Train humanoid robots for household tasks, aiming for full automation [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: The race for physical AI is heating up, with data becoming the new oil. Figure's massive dataset could accelerate the development of versatile household robots.

stories.title: Fake think tank floods web to poison chatbots.
stories.toc_summary: A think tank reportedly funded by Israel published 124 reports in 9 days, aiming to influence AI models' consensus by flooding training data.
stories.quick_take: A website disguised as a US think tank, reportedly funded by Israel, released 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words in just nine days [1]. The intent was not to inform human readers but to manipulate the data layer that AI chatbots draw from, effectively 'vaccinating' models with misleading content [1]. This new tactic highlights the vulnerability of AI systems to coordinated disinformation, raising concerns for businesses that rely on AI outputs for decision-making [1].

bullets.label: Scale:
bullets.text: 124 reports, 560k+ words in 9 days [1].

bullets.label: Method:
bullets.text: Flooding the web to shift what chatbots present as consensus [1].

bullets.label: Source:
bullets.text: Reported by The Guardian; allegedly funded by Israel [1].

bullets.label: Implication:
bullets.text: AI outputs can be manipulated; verifying sources becomes critical [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: For businesses using AI, this underscores the need for grounding and source verification to avoid acting on poisoned data.

editorial.title: AI's moat shifts to data and distribution.
editorial.intro: Today's stories span chips, robots, and disinformation, but a common thread emerges: the competitive edge in AI is moving from model quality to proprietary resources.
editorial.body: OpenAI's chip and Figure's dataset both underscore a pivot toward owning infrastructure and data. Leon Szeli's 'KI Burggraben' thesis—data and distribution—mirrors this shift. Meanwhile, China's robotics speed and Waymo's European expansion show that physical-world AI is entering a new phase. The fake think tank incident reminds us that with AI's growing influence, the integrity of data becomes paramount.
editorial.pull_quote: Models are becoming commodities; the real moat is proprietary data and a strong distribution network.
editorial.outro: As AI races forward, the winners will be those who control the scarce inputs—data, silicon, and physical presence—rather than just algorithms.

takeaway.label: IF YOU TAKE ONE THING FROM THIS
takeaway.text: For businesses, the path forward is clear: invest in proprietary data, own your distribution channels, and be wary of the data your AI consumes. The era of generic AI is ending; differentiation now comes from what you know and who you reach.
